newsitem.title: UK: U.S. data jolts Wall Street, European bourses.
newsitem.headline: U.S. data jolts Wall Street, European bourses.

text.p: Stronger-than-expected American housing data, which jangled market nerves over interest rate prospects, depressed U.S. bond and share prices on Tuesday and added to the weakness of European bourses.
"People are once again talking about higher interest rates in the U.S., which is not good news for stocks," one London dealer said.

The Dow Jones industrial average of leading U.S. stocks, down more than 30 points within minutes of opening to add to 36.52 points lost on Monday, later made a comeback and briefly scored limited gains.

The latest reading of the world's biggest economy, unwelcome news for U.S. markets fearing official action to damp things down, also weakened the dollar after a brief boost following a small cut in French interest rates.
November U.S. housing starts were reported to have jumped 9.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted 1.514 million. This was the strongest rise for 16 months and far exceeded market forecasts.

But market analysts said the U.S. central bank, the Federal Reserve, was expected to decide on Tuesday to hold interest rates unchanged amid hopes for steady economic growth. The jump in housing starts followed two months of declines.
The bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) is set to announce its rate decision at about 1915 GMT.
"No one is expecting a change in (U.S.) rates ahead of Christmas," a London share trader said. "If there is one, it will catch everybody by surprise."

European markets had already been under the weather after a reversal on Wall Street on Monday when news of a solid 0.9 percent gain in U.S. industrial output last month created tension ahead of the FOMC meeting.
Currency traders, meanwhile, were digesting pointers to German views on exchange rates after Friday's agreement on a European Union budget stability pact to back up a future single euro currency.
The Bundesbank's latest report said exchange rates broadly reflected fundamental factors and the mark had completely corrected a prolonged period of strength in recent years.
"The main thing underpinning the mark is that it now looks like the Germans are unhappy with the outcome of the EU summit," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.

The German central bank's chief economist, Otmar Issing, told the Financial Times he was not satisfied with a lack of automaticity in the stability pact underpinning planned European Economic and Monetary Union.
He lashed out at the European budget pact, saying the deal still held the risk that governments could be given political licence to overspend.

The London stock market, Europe's busiest, opened lower, depressed by a late sell-off in technology stocks in New York on Monday which neutralised much of the impact of Boeing's $13.3 billion acquisition of fellow aerospace giant McDonnell Douglas.
Takeover talk later briefly helped it revive from its lows before the U.S. data weighed in in the opposite directizon.
Investors are worried about a further slide on Wall Street and the chances of a year-end rally are fading, analysts said.
Frankfurt, down around 1.5 percent, showed the biggest drop of major bourses, with weakness of the dollar -- which sours prospects for Germany's many exporters -- a key depressant.
"We have lost what we gained yesterday but volumes are relatively weak. Most players have had enough and just want to celebrate Christmas," said one German share dealer.
French shares were also depressed and even a small Bank of France rate cut gave only brief relief.

The Bank of France trimmed its intervention rate to 3.15 percent from 3.20 and its less crucial five-to-10 day rate to 4.60 percent from 4.75. The mark was little changed against the French franc at 3.3756 versus 3.3760 late on Monday.
CURRENCIES AT 1530 GMT

The dollar was quoted around 1.5470 marks and 113.85 yen, compared with 1.5510 and 114.29 in late business on Monday. It had earlier topped 114 yen after a Japanese cabinet minister called for a slightly weaker yen.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1530 GMT
The FTSE 100 index of top British shares was down 11.6 at 3,982.2. In Frankfurt, the 30-share DAX ended floor trade 40.66 lower at 2,815.13 and was at 2,806 in later electronic trading.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index was down 27.68 at 2,194.89.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $368.20 in the afternoon, just below the morning setting of $368.30 but up from the previous $367.55 close. Silver edged up two cents to $4.82.
